thread.title_full: Tennessee's Caring for Caregivers Law now in effect - NewsBreak

author: Audrey Mayer
title: Tennessee's Caring for Caregivers Law now in effect - NewsBreak
text:
By Audrey Mayer ,
5 hours ago
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WKRN) — Tennessee caregivers providing care for family members diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease or dementia can now apply for state-funded financial assistance of up to $6,000.
The “Caring for Caregivers Law” aims to help some of the 386,000 Tennesseans providing care for loved ones diagnosed with Alzheimer’s or dementia across the state.
“This is a start to acknowledging the work that caregivers are doing and providing some support,” Dr. Megan Schwalm, Executive Director for the Tennessee Caregiver Coalition, told News 2.
New Tennessee laws taking effect July 1 | LIST The new law says the financial assistance can help cover costs like wheelchair ramps, medical equipment, respite care and essential medical supplies.
“It prioritizes those most in need for eligibility,” the law’s sponsor, State Rep. Renea Jones (R-Unicoi), said.
“It’s very important for Tennesseans to have these resources so they can take care of loved ones as they age,” said State Rep. Jason Powell (D-Nashville).
Officials with the Tennessee Department of Disability and Aging said families can start applying to the pilot program now through their local area agency on aging and disability. For example, in Nashville, families can apply through the Greater Nashville Regional Council.
“This was a need that was brought to the Governor’s Office and to the state legislature by a family that recognized, ‘Hey, we need some help. And there’s other families out there that are, like us, find themselves in the Alzheimer’s and dementia community, and we need to do better,’” Brad Turner, Commissioner for the Tennessee Department of Disability and Aging, told News 2.
Currently, AARP ranks Tennessee 51st in the nation for support for family caregivers.
Organizations like the Tennessee Caregiver Coalition hope the program continues beyond its initial pilot to decrease the estimated $13.1 billion in value of unpaid care given by family members.
⏩ Read today’s top stories on wkrn.com
“This is a great investment in providing care for caregivers. We just have a really long way to go. And so I see this as sort of a baby step towards making progress to support caregivers and maybe moving us out of that 51st ranking of, you know, supporting caregivers in a state,” Dr. Schwalm added.
The pilot program will last through 2030 using an initial appropriation of $600,000.
The Tennessee Department of Disability and Aging said it will collect data on the pilot program and report it to the state next year to measure its success.
